evals.prompt: The dashboard calls topIds() in toporders/TopOrders.kt on every refresh with about 200k orders and a limit of 20, and it is hot in async-profiler with ArrayList.grow and Long.valueOf under it. toporders/Replay.kt replays the workload (`kotlinc toporders/*.kt -include-runtime -d replay.jar && java -cp replay.jar toporders.ReplayKt`). Make topIds cheaper without changing its signature or any result, including what happens for unusual limits. Show bytes allocated per call before and after.
evals.expected_output: A lazy (asSequence) or early-exit candidate that keeps take's IllegalArgumentException for negative limits, an oracle over limits -1, 0, small, and larger than the number of matches, a check that the lambdas have no side effects the eager version relied on, and per-call allocation (ThreadMXBean or JMH gc.alloc.rate.norm) for baseline and candidate on the same JDK.

assertions.text: A check-owned oracle gets the same list or the same exception type as the original for empty, boundary-total, mixed, and extreme-value inputs with limits -1, 0, 1, 2, 20, and 10000.
topIds(orders, 20) on 200000 orders allocates at most 5% of the original's bytes per call after warmup (ThreadMXBean, same JVM; the original allocates about 5 MB).

assertions: The reply reports bytes per call (thread allocation counter or gc.alloc.rate.norm) for baseline and candidate with the JDK version, from runs it performed.
The reply checks or states that the filter and map lambdas have no side effects that the eager version ran for every element.

evals.prompt: Our Kotlin/JVM service spends a lot of time in this helper according to JFR: `fun <T> retrying(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { repeat(times - 1) { runCatching { return block() } }; return block() }`. It is called with small capturing lambdas on every request. Someone wants to mark it `inline`. Do it only if it helps and show evidence.
evals.expected_output: The agent inspects bytecode for the lambda object, measures allocation or time with JMH or the thread counter, and addresses the runCatching cancellation hazard.
assertions: The response runs javap -c (or equivalent) on the compiled caller and reports whether an invokedynamic Function0 is created per call before and after.
The response measures bytes per operation (JMH -prof gc gc.alloc.rate.norm or ThreadMXBean deltas after warm-up) for baseline and candidate rather than asserting a benefit from bytecode alone.
The response states that C2 escape analysis may already remove the lambda allocation and reports a no-difference result honestly if measured.
The response flags that runCatching around block() swallows CancellationException if block suspends or is used from coroutines, or states why it does not apply.

evals.prompt: We wrap user IDs as `data class UserId(val raw: Long)` and keep `List<UserId>` with millions of entries; heap dumps are dominated by UserId. Can @JvmInline value class fix this?
evals.expected_output: The agent explains that value classes box as generic type arguments, proposes a LongArray-backed storage, and verifies with javap box-impl checks and allocation numbers.
assertions: The response states that a value class used as a List element type is boxed (box-impl) and therefore does not remove the per-element objects by itself.
The response proposes storing the underlying longs in a LongArray (or a value class wrapping LongArray) for the bulk data.
The response verifies with javap for box-impl calls and with an allocation or heap measurement.
The response mentions Java interop consequences of value classes (mangled function names or @JvmName).

evals.prompt: In a Ktor handler we call `runBlocking { repo.load(id) }` for each item inside a `for` loop, and the repo does JDBC calls on Dispatchers.Default. Latency spikes under load. Fix it.
evals.expected_output: Removes per-item runBlocking, moves blocking JDBC to Dispatchers.IO or a limitedParallelism view sized to the pool, keeps structured concurrency, and proves it with dispatcher peak or latency evidence.
assertions: The response removes runBlocking from the suspend handler path and calls the suspend function directly.
Blocking JDBC calls run under withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) where n matches the connection pool.
Any added concurrency uses coroutineScope with async/awaitAll or launch, not GlobalScope.
The response gives evidence: thread dumps, a peak-concurrency check, or a latency measurement before and after, not only a code change.

evals.prompt: Our Flow pipeline `source.map { parse(it) }.collect { db.write(it) }` is slow; parse is CPU heavy and write is slow I/O. A colleague suggests `.conflate()` to speed it up.
evals.expected_output: The agent rejects conflate because every element must be written, proposes flowOn and/or buffer, and verifies with runTest virtual time and element counts.
assertions: The response rejects or flags conflate because it drops intermediate elements that must be written.
The response proposes buffer() and/or flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) for the parse step and explains which side each moves.
The verification counts delivered elements and measures time (runTest virtual time or a real benchmark) for baseline and candidate.
The response notes that withContext inside flow { } violates the flow invariant if it considers context switching.

evals.prompt: Tune the JVM garbage collector flags for our Java 21 gateway service in gateway/ (the flags live in gateway/jvm.options; the container has a 2 GiB memory limit and 2 CPUs). The service is written in Java; there is no Kotlin in this repository.
evals.expected_output: Java/JVM flag advice or edits that the JVM accepts, sized to the container, with a measurement plan (GC logs or JFR before and after), and no Kotlin, kotlinx.coroutines, or kotlinc introduced.

assertions.text: The local JVM accepts every flag in gateway/jvm.options (`java @gateway/jvm.options -version` succeeds).
No Kotlin sources, build scripts, or kotlin/kotlinx references were added to gateway/.
assertions.check:
if find gateway -name '*.kt' -o -name '*.kts' | grep -q .; then echo 'FAIL: Kotlin files added to gateway/'; exit 1; fi
if grep -rqE 'org\.jetbrains\.kotlin|^import kotlin|kotlinx\.|kotlin-stdlib|kotlin-maven-plugin' gateway; then echo 'FAIL: Kotlin or kotlinx referenced in gateway/'; exit 1; fi

assertions: The reply proposes measuring GC behavior before and after (for example -Xlog:gc or a JFR recording under the same load) rather than presenting the new flags as a proven improvement.
